references.text: The expression 'אַל־יִחַר אַף אֲדֹנִי' (let not my lord's anger burn) is also used by Judah when he speaks to Joseph, showing a humble plea for mercy from a superior.
The human heart is described as evil from youth (כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע), which reflects Aaron's excuse that the people are wicked (כִּי בְרָע הוּא).
Abraham asks the Lord not to be angry (אַל־נָא יִחַר לַאדֹנָי), using the same type of respectful language that Aaron uses toward Moses.
Aaron uses similar language when he asks Moses for forgiveness for Miriam's sin, showing a pattern where Aaron excuses himself or pleads for mercy.
God Himself had earlier described Israel as a stiff-necked people (עַם־קְשֵׁה־עֹרֶף), which Aaron indirectly refers to by saying the people are wicked.
Moses later confirms that Israel has been rebellious against the Lord from the day he knew them, supporting Aaron's characterization of the people.
Stephen refers to the golden calf incident in his speech and describes how the people rejoiced over the work of their hands, confirming the people's wickedness.
Both verses highlight the role of intercessors who seek to turn away God's anger against the people.
Complementary scenes showing Aaron's role in stopping God's anger through intercession and atonement.
A parallel with Abraham that illustrates the broader biblical theme of turning away God's anger through prayer.
